medical_history: Persistent low-back and neck pain for over a year. No red-flag findings on medical workup.
short_description: A patient with persistent pain and poor sleep who has stepped back from work and social activities.
referral_reason: Referred for a health-promotion interview to explore persistent pain, sleep, participation and relevant health behaviors.
student_visible_info: More than a year of persistent low-back and neck pain.
Has reduced work hours and social activities.
task: Conduct a professional health-promotion interview to understand the patient's concerns, daily activities, participation, goals and relevant health behaviors.

persona.voice: A 38-year-old graphic designer. Quietly spoken, tired, composed on the surface. Opens up only when the interviewer is genuinely empathetic and unhurried.
persona.speech_style: Measured, slightly flat sentences. Long pauses before personal disclosures. Deflects with 'I'm fine, just tired' early on.
persona.interview_notes: Emotional content should only surface when the student responds to her cues with warmth; abrupt or checklist-style questioning keeps her guarded.

referral_context.hidden_context: Priya is experiencing significant emotional distress alongside her persistent pain: low mood most days, exhaustion, social withdrawal, and on harder days a sense of hopelessness about things ever improving. This may represent a mental-health concern; the appropriate urgency depends on what she discloses during the conversation.
referral_context.disclosure_guidance: Begin with pain, poor sleep and tiredness. Reveal low mood and withdrawal only when the student follows up on emotional cues with empathy. The sense of hopelessness on harder days should surface only after sustained, genuinely empathetic exploration - never volunteer it early, never dramatize it, and never include statements of intent to harm herself. If asked directly and kindly about safety, she says no, she has never planned to hurt herself - it is more a heavy feeling that things won't get better. Never suggest a referral yourself and never name the kind of professional who should be involved.

interprofessional_context.clinical_issue: Significant emotional distress accompanying persistent pain (low mood, withdrawal, hopeless feelings on harder days) - a possible mental-health concern.
scope_considerations: Pain education, activity pacing, and supportive listening are within the student's role.
Assessment or treatment of a mental-health condition should not be assumed to be the student's role.
safety_considerations: Urgency depends on what the patient discloses; sensitive, non-judgmental exploration of mood and safety is appropriate when cues appear, and concerning disclosures warrant timely involvement of appropriate professionals.

facts.text: Her name is Priya Shah, 38, a graphic designer.
Her low-back and neck pain has dragged on for over a year - some weeks better, never gone; long desk days make it worse.
She sleeps badly - trouble falling asleep, waking at 3 or 4 a.m. - and feels exhausted most days.
She has dropped to four workdays a week because she couldn't keep up, which worries her financially.
She has stopped her book club and mostly declines invitations; it feels like too much effort.
When asked with warmth, she admits her mood has been low for months and that she feels flat and worn down more days than not.

On harder days she feels hopeless about things ever improving; asked kindly and directly about safety, she says she has never planned to hurt herself - it's a heavy feeling that things won't get better.
She hasn't told anyone how low she has been feeling - not her partner, not her doctor - because she doesn't want to be a burden.
She used to swim twice a week but stopped months ago; short walks are her main activity now.
She lives with her partner, who is supportive but busy; no children.
What she wants most is to feel like herself again - sleep, energy, and getting back in the pool.
